stem.en: A bat hunting in complete darkness sends out calls and turns in mid-air each time one comes back to it. Two moths are close by, one at 5 m and one at 5 cm, and the bat goes straight to the nearer one.

text.en: It measures how long each echo takes to come back, because the call travelling out and back covers a longer path to the further moth and so takes longer.
It measures how loud each echo comes back, because a sound spread over a larger area must reach the further moth more faintly.
It measures how high each echo comes back, because a moth nearer the ground throws the sound back at a steeper angle.
It measures how many echoes come back from each moth, because a larger object scatters a call into more separate returns.

explanation.en: The bat is reading the round trip, exactly as you did with your stopwatch on the cliff. The call goes out to the moth and back, so a moth at 5 m needs a journey of 10 m and a moth at 5 cm a journey of 10 cm, and the times differ by a factor of a hundred. Loudness falls with distance too, but a bat steering on loudness alone would be steering on how spread out the sound is rather than on how far away the prey is - and the time is the quantity that scales with the distance.

hints.en: The echo-ranging in this question measures the same round trip you measured with your stopwatch, and the speed of sound is the same on both legs.
Which of the four quantities grows in proportion to the distance out and back: loudness, height, a count of echoes, or time?
